teaser: How technical debt stalled the Open Security Summit's website and follow-up, what the repositories show, and why agents make a restart worthwhile.
core_idea: The Open Security Summit treated every participant as a presenter and its website was edited by its participants, but copying each year's site, adding exceptions and never refactoring froze the code, drove contributors away and left the follow-up unscaled; agents that map the data, personalise and follow up now make it worth restarting, in person, online and as a home for projects, if it is funded.

quotes.text: every participant was treated as a presenter.
Nobody had the time to change the structure, so everything new went into a structure that could not change.

figures.caption: Left: commits a quarter across the four summit websites, 19,045 in all, with spikes in the summit weeks of June 2018, 2019 and 2020. Right: the number of different people committing each year, from 180 in 2018 to 14 in 2024 and 2 in 2025.
Left: lines of Hugo template code, from about 5,200 in the 2018 site to about 9,600, flat from 2022. Right: content files in the current site, from 140 at the end of 2020 to 998 at the end of 2024.
Sessions on the current site by year and how many link a recording: 87 and 1 in 2020, 91 and 25 in 2021, 110 and 67 in 2022, 70 and 58 in 2023, 51 and 45 in 2024.

How the debt grew: a new summit copied last year's site, a new need added an exception, there was no time to refactor, every change got slower, and the loop repeated. The restart: agents map what is there, a personal path for each person, in person in London and online, and hosted open source projects.
